rv.q: Mr. Iverson gives a dynamic, compelling performance—he's essentially the whole show...
Yet “A Ghost in Your Ear” also feels timid in both form and themes.

But the story he’s telling, about a man returning to his dead estranged father’s spooky old manor house, is a pretty rote thing you might tell around a campfire, and Armitage’s visual jumpscares are infrequent.

One extremely slick attraction, A Ghost in Your Ear is a yummy piece of Halloween candy aimed for date nights and families with teens, because it’s ultimately an entertaining horror show where not a dirty word is ever heard.
This is a performance that demands to be both heard and seen.
Armitage, who wrote and directed A Ghost in Your Ear, has delivered a nifty little thriller just in time for Halloween.
Owing a debt to The Woman in Black, the script and direction are by Jamie Armitage, who keeps the pace from sagging, creating an intricate choreography between the actor and the gray human head mic.
A Ghost in Your Ear lives up to its name, eventually making the hairs on your neck stand up.
A Ghost In Your Ear combines effective sound design with classic horror tropes — a haunted manor, a debilitating storm, a dark past — to create a truly unique experience on stage.
For all its theatrical ingenuity, however, the show is ultimately more impressive for its technical rather than thematical elements.
It might startle at first sight, but it vanishes into the darkness without a trace.
All of the scares — and I could count them on exactly one hand — are visual.
This theatrical ghost story becomes like a super-spreader event, a spectacular, specter-filled sensation that will infect your waking and sleeping consciousness for days.
I am forced to give A Ghost in Your Ear my highest recommendation and urge you to experience it for yourself immediately.
A Ghost in Your Ear is a rare theatrical treat.
Even so, for those who enjoy being spooked, A Ghost in Your Ear sets a high bar for immersive theatrical storytelling.
It is worth an evening at the theatre if you enjoy a good horror story, an exceptional performance and mind-blowing audio technology.
Though A Ghost in Your Ear doesn’t meet expectations, its approach is undeniably inventive.

If the frights are milder than one might hope, the work surprisingly has something to say about the travails of fatherhood, while unintentionally delivering important lessons on the nature of live performance.
But in terms of plot and writing, the play falls flat.

cn.t: This binaural horror play earns praise for its innovative headphone-delivered scares and immersive sound design, though critics are divided on whether the audio gimmick compensates for a thin story.

vr.q: If you like horror and spooky things, especially with Halloween coming up, then you're probably gonna wanna check this one out.
I was bored by the story within the story. It just it wasn't that interesting of a ghost story to me.
